title: The Softest Ground
passage:
A playground surface is not engineered to feel soft. It is engineered to bring a falling head to rest slowly enough, and how slowly is decided by the tallest platform standing above it. Sanna Vikhaug, who tests surfaces for a certification lab, drops an instrumented headform onto sample beds and reads the deceleration off a curve; a bed that passes under a low toddler frame can fail badly under a three-meter tower, though nothing whatever about the material has changed. That is why the loose fills — bark, sand, engineered wood fiber — are neither the cheap compromise nor the villain they are usually taken for. Poured rubber and wood chips can both be built to meet the same fall height. The difference is that chips travel: children kick them out from under the swings, which is exactly where they are wanted, and a bed that met its rating in May may be two inches short of it by September unless somebody rakes it back.
— Halvor Reim, engineering notebook

questions.prompt: According to the text, what decides whether a playground surface is safe enough?

options.text: Which material is used, since poured rubber outperforms loose fills such as bark and wood chips wherever a site can afford it.
How soft the bed feels underfoot, since a surface that gives under a walking child will also cushion a falling one.
How gently it stops a falling head, judged against the tallest equipment above it, and whether it is kept at that depth.
How quickly it drains, since a waterlogged bed packs down over a season and hardens towards the ground beneath it.

questions.rationale: TYPE-001 direct detail, drawing on the two conditions the passage names. The text sets the standard as bringing 'a falling head to rest slowly enough', with the required slowness 'decided by the tallest platform standing above it', and then adds the maintenance condition — a bed that met its rating in May 'may be two inches short of it by September unless somebody rakes it back'; C paraphrases both. A = contradiction: the passage says the loose fills are 'neither the cheap compromise nor the villain they are usually taken for' and that rubber and chips 'can both be built to meet the same fall height', so material is not what decides. B = contradiction of the opening line: 'A playground surface is not engineered to feel soft' — feel underfoot is precisely the intuition the text overturns. D = outside_knowledge: drainage and waterlogging are a plausible real-world worry but appear nowhere in the text, which ties failure to fall height and lost depth.
